extracted.intended_audience: university students, faculty, administrators, and educators interested in the aims and curriculum of a University (mid-19th-century Catholic University context)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the aims, central subjects, and curriculum principles for the Faculty of Arts in a university — arguing for the primacy of the classical liberal arts and the integration of sacred and profane learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centrality of the Faculty of Arts in a University
rubrics_metrics.description: A University should be formally based in, and should emphatically live in, the Faculty of Arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newman observes that despite historical links with Theology, Law, and Medicine, the deliberate decision of those who considered the subject most deeply was that the Faculty of Arts is the foundation of a University; historically Arts existed before other faculties and the Masters of Arts were the ruling body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arts as the staple of the mental exercises proper to a University
rubrics_metrics.description: The studies which the Faculty of Arts embraces are 'almost the direct subject-matter and the staple of the mental exercises proper to a University.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On opening a School of Philosophy and Letters the focus should be on these studies because they constitute the core intellectual exercises that define university education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of education: strengthen, refine, and enrich the intellectual powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The simple question is how best to 'strengthen, refine, and enrich the intellectual powers' of students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subjects should be chosen for their power to cultivate the mind — not merely for producing useful facts or practical utility; the aim is mental formation rather than only material benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose subjects that provide the most robust discipline for the unformed mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction should prioritize those studies which 'provide the most robust and invigorating discipline for the unformed mind.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newman argues that, on available evidence and experience, the perusal of poets, historians, and philosophers of Greece and Rome accomplishes this purpose better than experimental sciences (which, though attractive and useful, lack comparable evidence of forming the intellect).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of the liberal arts against encroachment by newer sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: The Faculty of Arts and the classical course should not be 'detruded' by modern sciences or treated as secondary because newer philosophies have dazzling practical results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical experience shows that medieval Scholastic Theology, Law, and Medicine did not and should not supplant the liberal arts; similarly modern sciences should not replace classical training in the Arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classical literature (Greek and Roman) as the primary instrument of education
rubrics_metrics.description: The literature of Greece continued and enriched by Rome has been the instrument of education and the food of civilization from the first times down to this day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Canonical authors (Homer, Virgil, Horace, Cicero, the tragedians, etc.) function as long-standing text-books; their sustained use across centuries and across civilizations is evidence of their pedagogical value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use enduring texts that have stood the test of centuries
rubrics_metrics.description: Educational selections should favor works 'which have more or less been given from the earliest times, and are, in fact, in equal esteem and respect, in equal use now, as they were when they were received in the beginning.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newman cites the continued use of Homer, Virgil, Horace, Cicero, and others through many ages as a reason to retain them in curricula rather than replacing them with ephemeral works or untested innovations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include the Seven Liberal Arts as foundational curriculum
rubrics_metrics.description: The classical course of liberal education involved four principal studies — Grammar, Rhetoric, Logic, and Mathematics — and Mathematics subdivided into Geometry, Arithmetic, Astronomy, and Music, making the Seven Liberal Arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newman traces how these seven arts formed a 'definite school of intellect' and argues for their continued place as instruments of mental cultivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetoric and History as essential parts of training (oratory linked to political life)
rubrics_metrics.description: Oratory became a separate art (Rhetoric) and, being political in nature, presupposed or introduced the cultivation of History; thus history (Thucydides) became a special study informing oratory (Demosthenes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because rhetoric is tied to public and political life, curricula intended to form citizens and leaders should include instruction in rhetoric and the historical texts that foster it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of sacred (Christian) and profane (classical) learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Sacred learning (Jerusalem) and profane learning (Athens) are correlative and mutually complementary; both should be recognized and, where appropriate, integrated in a Catholic University.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newman stresses that Rome inherited and concentrated both traditions; to separate them is a regression. He suggests a distinct lecture could show in detail 'how faith operates by means of reason, and reason is directed and corrected by faith.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer long experience over novelty when choosing pedagogical methods
rubrics_metrics.description: The perusal of the poets, historians, and philosophers of Greece and Rome will accomplish intellectual formation 'as long experience has shown'; one should not substitute new methods merely because they are novel or dazzling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newman warns against assuming that the success of the Baconian/experimental method in its proper province justifies applying it wholesale to the cultivation of the intellect; experience should guide curricular choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: The classical canon as a unifying foundation for a common civilization
rubrics_metrics.description: The Classics and the studies they involve have been instruments of education which the civilized orbis terrarum has adopted, forming a common Thought and Civilization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection of a curriculum that reflects shared classical texts helps to form a common intellectual heritage and continuity across societies and ages.

rubrics_metrics.name: University governance and authority historically linked to the Masters of Arts
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically the Masters of Arts were the ruling and directing body; the success/popularity of other faculties (Law, Medicine) was viewed as an encroachment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This historical fact is used to argue that the Faculty of Arts should retain primacy in both teaching and governance, not be subordinated by professional or scientific faculties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literature is not merely stylish composition or conceits
rubrics_metrics.description: A critique of the view that fine writing is mainly a matter of 'conceits, fancies, and prettinesses' decked out in choice words — i.e., literature is not simply artificial stylistic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newman begins to argue that literature (Letters) should not be reduced to mere 'fine writing' or judged solely by translatability; its value lies deeper in content, tradition, and formative power (the discussion continues beyond the chunk).
